claims.text: OFFSET counts row positions over the rows the query sees when it runs; a row inserted or deleted (or leaving a filter) before the page position between two requests shifts later rows, so offset pages repeat or skip a row.
claims.source_hint: PostgreSQL docs 7.6 LIMIT and OFFSET; 13.2.1 Read Committed (each statement sees its own snapshot)

claims.text: PostgreSQL's default index kind (B-tree), including the one behind a primary key, keeps values in sorted order; with one on the sort column PostgreSQL can find the cursor value (id > X) and read forward from there.
claims.source_hint: PostgreSQL docs 11.2 Index Types (B-tree handles <, <=, =, >=, > and ordered output), 11.4 Indexes and ORDER BY

claims.text: Rows skipped by OFFSET still have to be computed inside the server, so a large OFFSET can be inefficient.

OrdersController.List (stage-2): [Authorize]; [FromQuery, Range(0, int.MaxValue)] int after = 0; [FromQuery, Range(1, MaxPageSize)] int limit = 20 (MaxPageSize 100); Forbid() when no current customer; calls repository.ListByCustomerAsync(customer.Id, after, limit).
EfOrderRepository.ListByCustomerAsync filters Where(o.CustomerId == customerId && o.Id > afterId), OrderBy(o.Id), Take(limit), with no Skip.
A negative after or a limit over 100 gets 400 through the Range checks and [ApiController]; Forbid() answers 403 for an authenticated caller.
claims.source_hint: ASP.NET Core docs: web-api/index.md Automatic HTTP 400 responses; ControllerBase.Forbid; lab curl
